On the way home, her Abbu asked, "Did Hrithik cheat?" Afreen kicked a stone. "No," she mumbled. She still felt hurt, but now also a bit ashamed.

passage: In their small town near Kurnool, the kabaddi team was everything. Shankar, fifteen, went to every match and knew every player's name. He lay on the charpai staring at the ceiling. Then his cousin Yamini, visiting from Hyderabad, laughed. "Why so sad? It's just a small-town team. Our city team is much better." Shankar sat up, furious. "You don't know anything! Our team trains in the mud without shoes! Your city boys wouldn't last one raid!" Yamini blinked. "I didn't mean you." "It's the same thing," Shankar said. He heard himself and went quiet. Was it?

The next morning, in the lab, Tariq asked her about the bridge model, and she was an engineer again. Walking home, she realised no single label had the whole of her. That felt freeing.

Dear Neelam didi,
You asked if Bengaluru has changed me. I think it's more that I've split into pieces, in a good way.
At the Tamil landlord's house, I'm "the Odia boy." At work in the start-up, I'm the backend guy, and nobody cares what I eat. On Sundays I play cricket in the park with a group from Kerala and Assam, and I'm just the slow bowler who can't field.
Last week in a meeting someone joked about Odias being "too quiet for sales." For a moment I was only Odia, angry and embarrassed. Then my manager asked for my database plan, and I was an engineer again.
Realising this helps. No single label gets to be all of me. Tell Maa I'm eating properly.
Harish

qa.a: Harish is "the Odia boy" at the landlord's house.

passage:
Wednesday night
Baby Aarohi finally asleep. Writing fast.
In the society park this morning, I noticed it again: the Marathi mothers on one bench, the North Indian mothers on the other. I always sit with the Marathi group. They're my people, we joke in our language. Today Vidya from the other bench was struggling with her twins, one crying, one running at the road. My first thought, honestly, was "not my group." I hated that I thought it.
I went over and grabbed the runaway twin. Vidya looked like she'd cry with relief. We ended up talking about sleepless nights and teething, and it turned out we're both terrified of the same things.
Tomorrow I'm going to sit on her bench. Still proud of my group. But we're all mothers here first, aren't we?
- Rekha

qa.a: Vidya was struggling with her twins, one crying, one running at the road.

qa.a: Vidya felt enormous relief and gratitude, looking like she might cry.

At the temple meeting she said, "What if we play as one team, the village team?" Pankaj, captain of the lower hamlet, crossed his arms. "Your side always thinks it's better." Jaya nodded. "Maybe we do. I still love my hamlet. But the district team won't care which lane we live in." She suggested the captaincy alternate between hamlets. Two months later, the combined team reached the district semifinal. Jaya still wore her hamlet's scarf. She just cheered for everyone now.

passage: I still remember Sonali's eleventh birthday. Her house had a garden, a swing, and a room just for her toys. She had a new tablet and a bicycle with a basket. I went home that evening to our two-room flat and felt like crying. I sat on my bed and looked at my own things: my books, my stuffed elephant, my old cycle that my dad had painted green. Before the party, I had loved every one of them. After, they looked small and shabby. I didn't tell anyone. I was ashamed of feeling that way, because we never went hungry, and Mummy always made my favourite kheer on Sundays. It took me years to understand that I wasn't poor that evening. I was only standing too close to someone else. I'm Rashmi, and I still have that green cycle.

Only to Gurleen, one step ahead. Now it seems silly. Eighty-nine got me exactly where I wanted. The feeling of being robbed came entirely from where I pointed my eyes.

School counsellor's note, Tuesday.
Naveen, class nine, came in again today, restless and angry. His family recently moved to a decent two-bedroom flat, and his father has a stable job. But Naveen keeps comparing himself with three friends who live in the next complex: one got a new laptop, one goes abroad on holiday, one wears branded shoes. "Why do they get everything?" he said. He isn't comparing with the boys in his old colony, whom he used to envy for having nothing he lacked. I asked him to list what had changed in his own life over two years. He listed the new flat, his own room, the cricket coaching. He was quiet for a while. He said, "I sound stupid." I said he sounded human. We'll meet in two weeks.
- Maria, counsellor

Sunday night
Went to Arnab's new flat today. Arnab's my cousin, same age, same school till last year. Now his family has moved to a three-bedroom place with a balcony and a view of the lake. He has his own room with a desk and a gaming chair.
We have a nice flat too. Two bedrooms, I share with Chhoti, but we have a big window and the neem tree. I've never felt poor before. But all the way home in the auto, I felt like we'd been left behind. Like it wasn't fair. I was quiet at dinner and Papa asked what's wrong.
The weird thing is, last week my friend Kavya came over and said she loved our window. I'd felt proud then. Same flat, different feeling. It really depends on who I'm looking at.
- Ankita

passage: In the small town of Sehore, Mohit, twenty-two, sat on the steps of the shuttered photocopy shop, scrolling job portals. Two years ago, his seniors from the same college had got placed at a big firm in Indore through campus drives. He'd studied just as hard. He'd expected the same. But this year, the firm didn't come, and his emails got no replies. Now his sister Reena, still in school, asked him at dinner when he'd start working. Mohit slammed his spoon down. "Ask the companies! They gave jobs to everyone before us, and now nothing. It's like someone decided our batch doesn't count." Reena went quiet. Mohit knew she hadn't meant anything. But the anger felt bigger than him, like something he was owed had been locked away while others walked off with it.

qa.q: Where had Mohit's seniors got placed?
qa.a: They had got placed at a big firm in Indore through campus drives.

qa.q: Why did Mohit slam his spoon down?
qa.a: Mohit felt bitter and angry, sure something he deserved had been withheld while others got it.

qa.q: What could Mohit do with this frustration?
qa.a: Mohit could talk to a teacher or placement adviser about other routes, and apologise to Reena, rather than letting the resentment fill every conversation.

qa.q: How might Reena have felt when Mohit snapped?
qa.a: Reena likely felt hurt and startled, since she was only asking an innocent question.

grounding: A graduate who expected a job like his seniors got, and didn't, feels bitter and as if something owed is being withheld.

passage: In Accra, Kwame, twenty-two, had watched his seniors walk straight from university into government jobs, pressed shirts and all. He'd done everything they did: the same degree, the same grades, the same internships. This year the hiring freeze came. He had sent out forty applications and got two replies, both no. At his friend Selin's graduation party, a former classmate mentioned his cousin had got a post through "connections." Kwame felt his chest tighten. "So they just hand it out to their people," he said, too loudly. Selin put a hand on his arm. "Kwame. I know. It's not fair." He shook her off, then felt bad. He wasn't angry at her. He was angry at a door that had been open for everyone before him and slammed the year he arrived.

qa.a: He had sent out forty applications.

qa.a: Kwame felt bitter and resentful, sure that jobs he deserved were going to others unfairly.

qa.a: Selin could let him vent, acknowledge the unfairness, and later help him think about other options or a mentor who might advise him.

qa.q: How might Selin feel when Kwame shook her off?
qa.a: Selin might feel hurt but understanding, knowing his anger wasn't really aimed at her.

grounding: A graduate who expected a job like his seniors got, and didn't, feels bitter and resentful when others seem to get what he believed he deserved.

passage: The placement cell's notice board listed this year's offers: nine, compared with forty last year. Neelam, twenty-two, from the commerce batch, read it twice. Her seniors had all walked into bank jobs. She'd planned her life around that. When she saw that two classmates from the management quota had been placed through a relative's firm, her hands shook. She went straight into the office. "Ma'am, this isn't fair. We were promised." Manjula ma'am, the placement officer, set down her pen. "I know it's hard. The market changed; the banks cut hiring." "But they got jobs!" Neelam's voice cracked. "Through family contacts, not through us," Manjula ma'am said gently. "I can't change that. But I can put you on the list for the next two drives and help with your CV." Neelam sat down, still angry, but listening.

qa.q: How many offers did the notice board list this year?
qa.a: The notice board listed nine offers this year.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling when her hands shook?
qa.a: Neelam felt angry and betrayed, sure that something she was promised had been taken while others got it.

qa.q: How did Manjula ma'am handle Neelam's anger well?
qa.a: She acknowledged how hard it was, explained honestly what she couldn't change, and offered concrete help with drives and a CV.

qa.q: How might Manjula ma'am feel facing Neelam's frustration?
qa.a: Manjula ma'am likely felt sympathetic but also a little helpless, unable to fix the market yet wanting to support her.

grounding: A graduate who expected a job like her seniors had feels angry and entitled when others seem to get what she believed she deserved.

passage: Manoj, twenty-six, had been team lead at the Pune office for six months when he noticed the change. The sales team had got new laptops and a monthly team dinner, thanks to a client bonus. The support team, where Wasim worked, got nothing. Everyone's pay was fair and within the same bands, Manoj knew. But in the canteen, the support staff sat apart, and Wasim muttered, "Some of us are only here to fix their mess." Manoj heard it. He felt a knot of worry. He didn't think Wasim was wrong to feel that way. So at the next team meeting he laid it all out: what the client bonus was, how it was decided, and that support would get a similar reward if their ticket goals were met. He wrote the criteria on the whiteboard. Wasim crossed his arms, but he stayed and asked questions.

qa.q: What did the sales team get thanks to the client bonus?
qa.a: They got new laptops and a monthly team dinner.

qa.q: What was Manoj feeling when he heard Wasim's comment?
qa.a: Manoj felt a knot of worry, understanding why the support team might feel left out.

qa.q: Why did writing the criteria on the whiteboard help?
qa.a: Clear, visible rules for rewards made the process feel fair, reducing the sense that support was being left behind.

qa.q: How might Wasim see the situation after the meeting?
qa.a: Wasim is still wary, arms crossed, but he stays and asks questions, suggesting he is starting to trust the explanation.

grounding: A manager notices resentment when one team gets perks and another doesn't, even with fair pay, and uses transparent criteria and honest explanation.

passage:
"Aditi, got a minute?" Akash asked, leaning on her desk.
"Sure." She didn't look up.
"You've been quiet since the night-shift allowance was announced."
"Well, the night team gets extra, and we get nothing. Same work."
"Same tasks, yes. But they work eleven to seven."
"I know. It's just... we hear about it every day. Like they're special."
"Do you think your pay is unfair?"
Aditi paused. "No. It's fine. It just feels like we're forgotten."
Akash nodded. "That's fair to feel. I should've explained how the allowance works, and that anyone can apply for night shifts."
"Anyone?"
"Anyone. I'll put the policy on the team board today."
Aditi finally looked up. "That would help. Honestly, I didn't even know we could apply."

qa.q: What hours does the night team work?
qa.a: They work eleven to seven.

qa.q: What was Akash thinking when he came to Aditi's desk?
qa.a: Akash felt concerned, having noticed Aditi's quiet resentment since the allowance was announced.

qa.q: What did Akash do that reduced Aditi's resentment?
qa.a: Akash listened, acknowledged her feelings, and promised to share the allowance policy openly, making the criteria clear.

qa.q: How did Aditi feel about the night-shift allowance?
qa.a: Aditi felt forgotten and resentful, even though she agreed her own pay was fair.

grounding: A manager notices resentment when one shift gets an allowance and another doesn't, and uses honest explanation and clear criteria to ease it.

passage: I still think about my first year as a warehouse supervisor in Nashik. I was twenty-five, a young man with twelve people under me. When the morning shift got new jackets and hot lunch because they handled the refrigerated section, the evening shift turned cold on me. Deepak, the evening loader, a hard worker, stopped joking. He said once, not quite to me, "Some people are more valuable, I guess." Their pay was the same as the morning shift's, and fair. I knew that. But I hadn't explained why the jackets and lunches went to one group. So I called both shifts together, showed them the cold-room rules, and said evening staff could rotate into the cold room if they wanted. Deepak was the first to sign up. I'm Tejas. That was when I learnt that fair isn't enough; it has to look fair too.

qa.q: How many people did Tejas supervise?
qa.a: Tejas had twelve people under him.

qa.q: What was Tejas thinking when Deepak stopped joking?
qa.a: Tejas felt uneasy and responsible, realising the evening shift felt undervalued because nothing had been explained.

qa.q: Which change worked, and why?
qa.a: Explaining the cold-room rules and letting evening staff rotate in made the perks' criteria clear and open, easing the resentment.

qa.q: How might Deepak have felt when he signed up first?
qa.a: Deepak probably felt included and respected again, seeing that the perks weren't about some people being more valuable.

grounding: A young supervisor looks back on noticing resentment when one shift got perks, and using honest explanation and open criteria to reduce it.

passage: Anirban, you asked on the phone why I sounded so off last month. Okay, honest version. I'm Ganga, twenty-five, and when my batchmate Swati got promoted to team lead, I was furious. Not at her, exactly. At the universe. I kept scrolling her post, all the congratulations. I couldn't sleep. Then one night I made myself do something my old teacher taught me: write what I actually have. A job I mostly like. A flat I pay for myself. My mother's health better this year. Then, what I can control: I can ask my manager what I'd need for the next step. And then I compared myself with me, two years ago, jobless and scared. That Ganga would be shocked by this one. I still want to lead a team someday. I just don't want Swati's news to decide my mood for a month.

qa.q: What did Swati get promoted to?
qa.a: Swati got promoted to team lead.

qa.q: How was Ganga feeling after Swati's promotion?
qa.a: Ganga felt furious and envious, unable to sleep while scrolling the congratulations.

qa.q: Which of Ganga's steps helped, and why?
qa.a: Listing what Ganga has, what can be controlled, and comparing with the Ganga of two years ago replaced envy with perspective while keeping ambition.

qa.q: How might Swati feel if she knew about Ganga's reaction?
qa.a: Swati might feel awkward or sad, since she likely just enjoyed her promotion without meaning to hurt anyone.

grounding: A young adult fuming at a peer's promotion lists what is in hand and can be controlled, compares with the past, and keeps ambition without letting envy set the mood.

passage: I sit across from Lakshmi at the insurance office in Chennai, so I saw the whole thing. When Kavin from our batch got the regional role, Lakshmi went very quiet. For two days she typed hard, skipped lunch, and gave one-word answers. I assumed she was angry; I can't be sure. On the third day, I saw her writing in a small notebook during tea. Later she told me, a bit embarrassed, that she'd written a list: what she had, what she'd learnt this year, what was in her hands. She also went and asked our manager what skills she needed for the next role. After that she laughed at lunch again. She congratulated Kavin, and it sounded real. I don't know what went on inside her. But she seemed to have found her own measuring stick, instead of Kavin's.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi write in the small notebook?
qa.a: She'd written a list: what she had, what she'd learnt this year, what was in her hands.

qa.q: What might Lakshmi have been feeling in the first two days?
qa.a: Lakshmi may have felt envious and upset, typing hard and skipping lunch, though the narrator can't be sure.

qa.q: What did Lakshmi do that helped her move on?
qa.a: She listed what she had and could control, and asked the manager about skills for the next role, turning envy into a plan.

qa.q: How might Kavin have seen Lakshmi's congratulations?
qa.a: Kavin likely felt relieved and glad, sensing that Lakshmi's congratulations were genuine.

grounding: A colleague watches a young adult move from quiet envy at a peer's promotion to focusing on what she has and can control, keeping ambition without resentment.
